flashcards.q: What is the difference between load and throughput?
flashcards.a: Load is how many requests arrive per second. Throughput is how many actually get finished per second.
flashcards.more: In a healthy system the two are equal: whatever arrives gets finished. Once load goes past capacity, throughput stops rising and the extra requests pile up in line. The throughput graph flattens while the latency graph climbs steeply.

flashcards.q: What is latency?
flashcards.a: The total time from sending a request to getting the reply: waiting in line plus the actual work.
flashcards.more: This is the only number the user feels. Even when the work takes the same time, a busy server adds waiting in line and latency grows. It is usually measured in milliseconds (ms).

flashcards.q: Why is judging a system by its average latency a mistake?
flashcards.a: The average hides slow requests behind the fast ones. Even with a healthy-looking average, 1-5% of users can have a terrible experience.
flashcards.more: If 95 people are served in 10 minutes and 5 in an hour, the average is 12.5 minutes, yet 5 people were badly served. That is why latency is always read as percentiles: p50, p95, p99. More in [[observability/metrics-slos/average-lies|metrics and SLOs]].

flashcards.q: p99 latency is 2 seconds. What does that mean?
flashcards.a: 99% of requests finished within 2 seconds; the remaining 1% took even longer.
flashcards.more: Sort all requests by time, and the value at the 99% position is p99. Likewise p50 (the median) is the middle value and p95 the value at 95%. With 1 million requests a day, that 1% is 10,000 slow requests.

flashcards.q: Why does tail latency (p99) matter even though it sounds rare?
flashcards.a: A page made of many internal calls quickly becomes likely to hit at least one slow call: with 20 calls, about 18%.
flashcards.more: If each call is fast 99% of the time, the chance that all 20 are fast is 0.99 to the power of 20, about 82%. In the other 18% of pages at least one call is slow, and the whole page waits on it. Heavy users also land in the tail more often.

flashcards.q: What does Little's Law say?
flashcards.a: L = λ × W: the average number of requests in flight = requests arriving per second × the average time one request takes.
flashcards.more: If 2 people enter the restaurant each minute and each stays 30 minutes, 60 are always inside. In an app, this L tells you how many PHP-FPM workers or database connections you need. The formula holds while the system is in a steady state, meaning what arrives also gets finished.

flashcards.q: 200 requests per second, average latency 0.25s. How many PHP-FPM workers do you need?
flashcards.a: 200 × 0.25 = 50 requests in flight, so at least 50 workers; with 20% headroom, about 60.
flashcards.more: In PHP-FPM every running request occupies one worker. If latency rises to 1 second, the same load needs 200 workers, which is why a slow database fills up every worker so fast. Before adding workers, check that they fit in RAM.

flashcards.q: What is a bottleneck, and what happens if you speed up anything else?
flashcards.a: The slowest step, or the first to fill up. Speeding up anything other than the bottleneck barely changes the total speed.
flashcards.more: If everyone is stuck at the cash counter, adding waiters doesn't shorten the line. If 2.5 of an app's 3 seconds go into one query, doubling the app servers doesn't help and only adds pressure on the database. Fix one bottleneck and the next one shows up elsewhere, so measure again.

flashcards.q: What happens to latency once a server is more than 80% busy?
flashcards.a: A line starts to form, and latency doesn't rise steadily, it jumps. Near 100%, the wait becomes unbounded.
flashcards.more: In a simple queue model where the work takes 10ms, latency is 20ms at 50% busy, 100ms at 90% and 200ms at 95%. That is why capacity planning treats 70-80% utilization as the limit, leaving room for sudden bursts.

flashcards.q: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows "Seq Scan" for a one-row lookup on a big table. What now?
flashcards.a: The database read every row. Add an index on the column in the WHERE clause, then run EXPLAIN again: it should say Index Scan.
flashcards.more: An index is like a phone book's alphabetical order. Build it with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in a migration, so live writes aren't blocked. The price is disk space and a little extra work on every write, so index the columns your slow queries filter on, not all of them.

flashcards.q: What is "blast radius" in system design?
flashcards.a: How much of the system a single failure or break-in can damage. Splitting parts onto separate machines, networks and credentials makes it smaller.
flashcards.more: On one box with the app, database, photos and backups together, one hole in the upload form reaches everything. After the split, an attacker who gets into the app still has to break into the database, the storage and the backups separately.

flashcards.q: Why is a backup stored on the same disk as the database not a real backup?
flashcards.a: The same disk failure, break-in or mistaken delete that hits the database hits the backup. A backup must live somewhere else.
flashcards.more: One disk is one failure. Push the backup to another place, with a key that can add files but not delete them, and switch on versioning or Object Lock. See [[recovery/backups-restore/backup-that-never-restored|backups and the 3-2-1 rule]].

flashcards.q: Name three things a single server shares between the app, the database and the files.
flashcards.a: The door (one break-in reaches all), the CPU and RAM (one heavy job slows all) and the disk (one full or dead disk takes all).
flashcards.more: A fourth is the calendar: you cannot patch or scale one part without touching the others. The split gives each part its own door, its own resources and its own failure.

flashcards.q: How do you keep a MySQL or PostgreSQL server off the public internet in its own config?
flashcards.a: MySQL: `bind-address` set to the private IP. PostgreSQL: `listen_addresses` set to the private IP, and a `pg_hba.conf` line limited to the app subnet.
flashcards.more: Keep the database port closed in the firewall or security group too. Check from outside with `nc -vz <public-ip> 3306`: it must fail. On a managed database, choose "not publicly accessible" and allow only the app's security group.

flashcards.q: What rights should the running app's database user have?
flashcards.a: Only what the code does at runtime: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on its own database. No DROP, ALTER or CREATE, and no global rights.
flashcards.more: A web shell that gets into the app inherits the app's database rights. With `shop_app` it can still read and change rows, but it cannot drop or alter tables. Least privilege limits the damage, it does not remove it.

flashcards.q: Why run migrations with a different database user than the app?
flashcards.a: Migrations need to change the schema, the app does not. Keeping the powerful user in the deploy pipeline stops a script in the app from using it.
flashcards.more: The deploy step runs `DATABASE_URL="$MIGRATE_DATABASE_URL" php bin/console doctrine:migrations:migrate --no-interaction`. The price is a second user and password to keep and rotate.

flashcards.q: What is "defense in depth"?
flashcards.a: Several independent locks in a row, each designed on the assumption that the one before it has already failed.
flashcards.more: Safe uploads stop the shell. A private database stops the outside world. Least privilege limits what a shell that got in can do. Off-box backups let you recover if everything else fails. Any single lock will fail one day, so the rest must hold.

flashcards.q: How do you stop an uploaded `shell.php` from running in nginx?
flashcards.a: Pin `/uploads/` with `location ^~` and deny `.php` inside it, pass only `index.php` to PHP-FPM, or store uploads outside `public/`.
flashcards.more: Also check the real type and size on the server, and save under a random name such as `Uuid::v7()`, not the visitor's file name. The safest place for uploads is object storage, where nothing can ever run as code.

flashcards.q: What does splitting the database onto its own host cost per query?
flashcards.a: A network hop, typically about 1 ms inside one data center, against well under 0.1 ms on the same box. 200 queries add about 200 ms.
flashcards.more: One query is harmless, but an N+1 page multiplies the hop. Load the rows in one JOIN. The split also adds more parts to run and watch, a new failure (the network between tiers) and a bigger monthly bill. When one box is still fine, see [[scaling/horizontal-vertical/bigger-or-more|vertical vs horizontal scaling]].

flashcards.q: What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling?
flashcards.a: Vertical = more CPU/RAM in the same machine. Horizontal = adding more machines running the same app.
flashcards.more: Vertical doesn't change your code so it's easy, but there's no path past the biggest machine, and if it dies everything stops. Horizontal has almost unlimited capacity and the rest keep running when one dies, but the app must be stateless and you need a load balancer.

flashcards.q: What does a stateless app mean?
flashcards.a: No server keeps user state (sessions, files) inside itself; any request can go to any server.
flashcards.more: State lives in shared places: sessions in Redis, files in object storage, data in the database. Then you can add or remove servers without losing anything, and that is the core requirement of horizontal scaling. More in [[thinking/serverless-stateless/logged-out-randomly|stateless design]].

flashcards.q: On two servers, users keep getting logged out. What is the likely cause?
flashcards.a: Each server stores sessions on its own disk. The second server doesn't recognize the first one's sessions.
flashcards.more: The fix is to keep sessions in one shared place; in Symfony that is `handler_id: '%env(REDIS_URL)%'`. Sticky sessions can hide the symptom too, but if the server dies the sessions are lost, so a shared store is the right way.

flashcards.q: What goes wrong with horizontal scaling if uploads are saved in `public/uploads`?
flashcards.a: The file exists only on the server that received it; a request to another server gets a 404.
flashcards.more: Files belong in object storage (S3-compatible). With Flysystem in Symfony you can switch between local disk and S3 with the same code. Put the file's key or URL in the database, not a server path.

flashcards.q: Why can't autoscaling absorb a sudden spike?
flashcards.a: Measuring the load, deciding, starting the server and warm-up together take several minutes. The old servers can collapse in that time.
flashcards.more: Autoscaling is great for slowly growing crowds. For known jumps, like a Black Friday sale or a TV ad, raise the minimum count in advance. Add a rate limit and load shedding, and the first few minutes of the wave are survivable.

flashcards.q: Why does adding app servers lead to "too many connections" in the database?
flashcards.a: Every worker on every server takes one connection. More servers push the total past the database's max_connections.
flashcards.more: 20 servers x 25 workers = 500 connections, while the database may be stuck at 200. The fix is a pooler like PgBouncer, which turns many client connections into just a few real ones. It comes with limits, covered in the next card.

flashcards.q: What breaks when PgBouncer runs in transaction pooling mode?
flashcards.a: Anything that assumes one connection stays yours: server-side prepared statements, SET, session advisory locks, LISTEN/NOTIFY, temp tables.
flashcards.more: Transaction mode lends a connection for one transaction only, then gives it to someone else. A prepared statement made on one connection is missing on the next. Use `SET LOCAL` inside transactions, and send migrations and LISTEN/NOTIFY straight to Postgres.

flashcards.q: In Symfony behind PgBouncer you see "prepared statement does not exist". What is the fix?
flashcards.a: Set PDO::ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES to true in the Doctrine dbal options, or on PgBouncer 1.21+ set max_prepared_statements.
flashcards.more: With emulation, PDO builds the query with escaped values and sends it in one go, so no statement is left on a connection that the next transaction might not get. The price is that Postgres can't reuse a parsed plan.

flashcards.q: When the database is slow, what is the right order of scaling steps?
flashcards.a: Fix queries, cache, read replicas, bigger machine, and shard last. The cheapest step comes first.
flashcards.more: Sharding splits the data, so cross-shard queries, transactions and operations all become far more complicated. Most apps go a very long way with the first three steps. More in [[data/sharding/last-resort|sharding]].

flashcards.q: What is a single point of failure (SPOF)?
flashcards.a: A part that stops the whole system when it dies, because it has no backup copy.
flashcards.more: People often add app servers and think everything is safe, but a lone load balancer, a lone database primary or a single data center is still a SPOF. Ask each part "what happens when you die?" and for any answer of "everything stops", add a second copy.

flashcards.q: How do you stop the load balancer itself from being a SPOF?
flashcards.a: Run two LBs and let the survivor take over the same IP (keepalived/VRRP), or use a cloud managed load balancer.
flashcards.more: In an active-passive pair one LB works while the other sends and listens for heartbeats. If the main one goes quiet for about 3 seconds, the second grabs the floating IP. A cloud managed LB already runs in several places, so on a cloud it is usually the easy route.

flashcards.q: What does an active/standby load balancer pair cost, and how can it fail?
flashcards.a: You pay for an idle second box with no extra capacity. Requests in flight are lost, and a broken link between the two can make both claim the IP.
flashcards.more: The standby only waits, so a pair gives survival, not more throughput. Failover takes a few seconds, and anything in flight at that moment is dropped. If A and B lose contact but both are alive, both claim the IP (split brain). Many clouds also block VRRP, so use the managed LB there.

flashcards.q: Round robin, least connections, weighted: which one when?
flashcards.a: Round robin takes turns, so it piles up on long requests. Least connections suits uneven request times, weighted suits unequal servers.
flashcards.more: When all requests are about equally short, round robin is the simplest and good enough. When some requests, like uploads or report exports, run for seconds on end, least connections is better. With unequal servers (2 cores vs 8) set a weight such as `weight=3`; in nginx the two can work together.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between passive and active health checks?
flashcards.a: Passive: a server is dropped when real requests fail. Active: the LB itself calls /healthz regularly, without waiting for real requests.
flashcards.more: Free nginx does passive checks with `max_fails` and `fail_timeout`; active checks are in HAProxy, nginx Plus or a cloud LB. With an active check, the first user doesn't have to be the victim of a failed request.

flashcards.q: What is the danger of calling the database in a health check?
flashcards.a: When the database has trouble, every server looks sick at once, the LB removes them all, and a small problem becomes a full outage.
flashcards.more: The LB's health check should answer "can this server take requests?", which is usually a cheap check of the server's own state. Watch the database's state with separate metrics and alerts. More in [[observability/health-alerts/alarm-that-always-rings|health checks and alerts]].

flashcards.q: What is the main difference between L4 and L7 load balancers?
flashcards.a: L4 looks only at IP and port and forwards TCP. L7 opens up the HTTP, so it can decide by path, header and cookie.
flashcards.more: L4 is fast and works for any TCP protocol (databases, Redis). L7 uses more CPU, but it can do TLS termination, path routing and header injection. In front of a web app you normally put L7.

flashcards.q: What are sticky sessions, and why avoid them?
flashcards.a: Always sending the same user to the same server. It unbalances the load and loses sessions when a server dies.
flashcards.more: Sticky sessions really just hide the symptom of state kept inside the server. Move the session to Redis and stickiness isn't needed, so the LB can split the load truly evenly. With ip_hash there is also the risk of thousands of users behind a NAT landing on one server.

flashcards.q: How do you remove the need for sticky sessions in Symfony?
flashcards.a: Set `framework.session.handler_id` to a Redis URL, so any server can read any session. Then use least_conn instead of ip_hash.
flashcards.more: The price is one extra network call to Redis per request, and Redis becomes a new single point of failure, so give it a replica. With the session outside, a server can die or be deployed and nobody gets logged out.

flashcards.q: What goes wrong when you pick cache nodes with hash(key) % N?
flashcards.a: When N changes, nearly every key changes node. Going from 4 to 5 nodes makes 80% of keys miss.
flashcards.more: The remainder rule depends on N, so changing N reshuffles almost every key. Most of the cache misses at once and piles pressure on the database. That's why cache clusters avoid this rule.

flashcards.q: How does the ring in consistent hashing work?
flashcards.a: Nodes and keys are both hashed onto a circle. A key belongs to the first node clockwise from it.
flashcards.more: The whole hash range (say 0 to 2^32) is treated as a circle. Reaching the end of the circle, you go back to the start (wrap-around). So the split depends on where the nodes sit on the circle, not on how many nodes there are in total.

flashcards.q: How many keys move when a node joins or leaves the ring?
flashcards.a: On average about 1/N of them, only the slice next to that node. Nothing else changes.
flashcards.more: A new node takes a slice from the node right after it. When a node leaves, its slice goes to the next node clockwise. So going from 4 to 5 nodes moves about 20% of keys, instead of the 80% of hash % N.

flashcards.q: What is a virtual node, and why is it needed?
flashcards.a: One real node placed at many positions on the ring. It makes the split of keys almost equal.
flashcards.more: With one position per node, luck with the gaps makes the split uneven. Give each node 100-200 positions and the law of averages evens it out. When a node dies its keys spread over all the nodes, and a bigger machine can be given more vnodes for a bigger share.

flashcards.q: How can a bigger machine take a bigger share on the ring?
flashcards.a: Give it more virtual nodes, for example weight 2 means 300 positions instead of 150. It then owns about twice as many keys.
flashcards.more: A weight is just a vnode count. In the HashRing above, `add('big-1', 2)` places twice as many positions for that node. Nothing else changes: lookups, wrap-around and removal work as before.

flashcards.q: When looking up a key on the ring, what do you do with the sorted list?
flashcards.a: Binary-search for the first position greater than or equal to the key's hash; if there is none, wrap back to the start of the list.
flashcards.more: The positions are sorted, so the search is O(log n). In PHP, `$lo % count($positions)` does the wrap-around. Every client must use the same hash function, the same node names and the same vnode count.

flashcards.q: Does Redis Cluster use a ring?
flashcards.a: No. Redis Cluster uses 16384 fixed hash slots; slot = CRC16(key) % 16384, and each slot belongs to one node.
flashcards.more: When you add a node, whole slots move from one node to another. The idea is the same: don't tie keys directly to nodes, put a layer in between, so that few things move when nodes change. More in [[data/sharding/last-resort|sharding]].

flashcards.q: Why doesn't consistent hashing fix the hot key problem?
flashcards.a: A key always goes to one single node. The ring spreads keys evenly but doesn't look at how often each key is read.
flashcards.more: If every user reads one viral product key, that node burns. The fixes: a short-lived local cache inside the app, or several copies of the key (`key#0` to `key#7`, each landing on a different node; reads pick one at random, writes update all). The price is more writes and copies that can briefly disagree.

flashcards.q: Why do you need leader election, and what is split brain?
flashcards.a: When only one party may do a job, you must pick one. If the network splits and both halves think they're the leader, that is split brain.
flashcards.more: From the outside you can't tell whether a server has died or is just stuck. So instead of deciding alone, you choose the leader by a majority vote. Otherwise the same salary, the same email or the same job runs twice.

flashcards.q: What is a quorum, and how big is it for N nodes?
flashcards.a: A majority: N/2 + 1 (integer division). 2 for 3 nodes, 3 for 5 nodes, 4 for 7 nodes.
flashcards.more: A decision passes only when a quorum agrees. If the network splits in two, the halves can't both be a majority, so you never get two leaders at the same time.

flashcards.q: Why do consensus clusters use an odd number of nodes, like 3 or 5?
flashcards.a: An extra node in an even count adds no tolerance. 4 nodes survive only 1 failure, same as 3, but cost more.
flashcards.more: With 3 nodes the quorum is 2, and 1 can die. With 4 nodes the quorum is 3, and still only 1 can die. With 5 nodes the quorum is 3, and 2 can die. More nodes means talking to more members on every decision, so it gets slower.

flashcards.q: How does Raft work in a nutshell?
flashcards.a: One leader takes all writes and sends the log to followers; a write is final when a majority acks. If the leader goes quiet, a vote elects a new one.
flashcards.more: Every election has a term number, and in each term a member casts a single vote. Paxos gives similar guarantees, but Raft was designed to be easy to understand and to build. More in [[data/consistency-models/time-travelling-page|consistency models]].

flashcards.q: What are etcd and ZooKeeper used for?
flashcards.a: Consensus-based services for keeping small but critical data (config, leaders, locks) reliably. etcd uses Raft, ZooKeeper uses Zab.
flashcards.more: Kubernetes keeps all its state in etcd. You won't write Raft yourself; you use these for leader election, locks and service discovery. They aren't a place for big data: little data, high reliability.

flashcards.q: What are the three rules for using Symfony Lock?
flashcards.a: Set a TTL, call refresh() during long jobs, and release() in a finally block. Leave the TTL out and Symfony uses 300 seconds, so a dead server blocks the job for 5 minutes.
flashcards.more: Create the lock with `$factory->createLock($name, ttl: 60)` and return if `acquire()` fails. A lock only gives the "don't run it twice" convenience; where money or stock is involved you need a fencing token or idempotency.

flashcards.q: What does a fencing token do?
flashcards.a: An increasing number is handed out with the lock, and the storage rejects any older (lower) number. So an expired lock holder can't do damage.
flashcards.more: A lock holder stuck in a pause doesn't know its lock is gone. So the final check lives in the storage: `WHERE last_token <= :token`. The token must be bumped in the same atomic step as the lock grant. etcd's revision and ZooKeeper's zxid give exactly this kind of token.

flashcards.q: What happens to a consensus cluster that loses its majority?
flashcards.a: It stops accepting writes. It prefers being unavailable to risking two leaders, so a 5-node cluster needs at least 3 nodes alive.
flashcards.more: This is the price of the quorum rule. With 5 nodes, 2 can die and it carries on. With 3 dead, the 2 survivors can't form a majority, so they wait until enough nodes come back. Stopping is safe; deciding on their own would risk split brain.

flashcards.q: What is replication lag?
flashcards.a: The time gap between a write on the primary and its arrival on the replica. During it, the replica shows stale data.
flashcards.more: Lag typically grows during heavy bursts of changes or when a replica is slow. Reading from replicas to share the read load means accepting the risk of stale data, so lag should always be measured and alerted on. More in [[data/replication/one-copy-is-risky|replication]].

flashcards.q: What kinds of trouble do users see from replication lag?
flashcards.a: They don't see their own writes, data goes back in time (monotonic reads break), and events appear out of order.
flashcards.more: Placing an order and seeing "no such order" is the first kind. The second happens when two replicas have different lag: one shows new data, the other old. In the third, the answer arrives before the question.

flashcards.q: How do you guarantee read-your-writes?
flashcards.a: After a user writes, serve their reads from the primary for a while, or return the new data in the POST response itself.
flashcards.more: In Symfony you can set a `last_write` cookie in the write response, and on reads check it and choose the primary connection for 5 seconds. Critical reads, like money or stock, are best always served from the primary.

flashcards.q: During dual write, which is the source of truth, the old or the new?
flashcards.a: The old one, until reads move over. If a write to the new one fails, log it and queue a repair; the user's action isn't blocked.
flashcards.more: The two writes are separate, so there is no guarantee they both succeed or both fail. Verification and backfill fill that gap later. The new place becomes the truth only after cutover.

flashcards.q: What is the correct order for moving big data?
flashcards.a: Build the new place, dual write, backfill, verify, move reads step by step, and retire the old one last.
flashcards.more: Without dual write first, writes that arrive during the backfill are lost. Reads move over starting at 1% and growing in steps, so that few users suffer if a problem shows up. Keep the old place for a while as a way back.

flashcards.q: What are the four rules of a backfill command?
flashcards.a: Small batches, keyset (id > last), idempotent INSERT (ON CONFLICT), and slow down when replica lag grows.
flashcards.more: OFFSET gets slow deep into a table, hence keyset. Thanks to ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, the command can safely be stopped and rerun. A pause after each batch keeps the pressure on the live site under control.

flashcards.q: If the counts of two tables match, is the copy correct?
flashcards.a: No. A count only matches numbers. To match values, use a checksum by id range or a shadow read.
flashcards.more: Two tables can have the same count even if one row says 'paid' and the other 'pending'. Matching checksums by range tells you exactly which slice differs, so you only need to copy that part again.

flashcards.q: How do you stop a user seeing time go backwards across replicas?
flashcards.a: Pin each user to one replica, for example user id modulo the number of replicas. One replica only moves forward, so what they see never jumps back.
flashcards.more: Without pinning, one refresh may hit a replica that has the new post and the next refresh one that doesn't. Pinning fixes the choice per user. The price: if that replica dies, its users move to another one and may see an older copy once, and the load can be uneven.

flashcards.q: In a migration, why does dual write upsert while the backfill uses DO NOTHING?
flashcards.a: A row can change while the backfill copies it. The upsert puts the newest value in the new table, and DO NOTHING stops the backfill's older copy from overwriting it.
flashcards.more: Picture the order: the backfill reads a row, the customer changes it, dual write stores the new value, and only then does the backfill insert its old copy. With DO NOTHING that insert is skipped and the newer value stays. If dual write only updated, it would find no row yet and the change would be lost.

flashcards.q: What are C, A and P in CAP?
flashcards.a: C: every read sees the latest write. A: every live node answers every request. P: the system keeps working even when communication between nodes is cut.
flashcards.more: Here C means linearizable consistency, not the C in ACID (obeying the rules). When a partition comes, you can't keep C and A together, so one must go. With no partition, you have both.

flashcards.q: What exactly is a partition?
flashcards.a: Nodes can't reach each other. A cut cable, a failed switch, or a link so slow it times out: all are partitions.
flashcards.more: In a 30-second GC pause, a server looks dead to the others. Slow and dead can't be told apart, so you design for it as a partition too. It is rare, but a big system does see it.

flashcards.q: How do CP and AP behave, with examples?
flashcards.a: CP: in a partition, if it can't give the right answer it returns an error or waits (balance, stock). AP: it always answers, though some answers may be stale (likes, feed).
flashcards.more: In CP the majority side stays up and the minority side stops. In AP both sides keep accepting writes and reconcile when the line is back. The choice is made per feature, not for the whole database. More in [[data/consistency-models/time-travelling-page|consistency models]].

flashcards.q: What does PACELC say?
flashcards.a: If there is a Partition, Availability or Consistency; Else, Latency or Consistency.
flashcards.more: CAP only talks about the time of the split. But most of the time the network is fine, and even then writing with everyone's agreement costs latency. PACELC names that second choice too.

flashcards.q: Why are multi-region quorum writes slow even when the network is healthy?
flashcards.a: Agreement from a distant region takes time because of the speed of light. Keeping answers correct is paid for in latency.
flashcards.more: A quorum across 3 AZs in one city is around 6ms, but across three continents it can take over 100ms. That's why a common tactic is to keep a user's writes in the region where that user is.

flashcards.q: Which features do you make CP and which AP?
flashcards.a: CP when wrong data costs money, stock or legal trouble. AP when slightly stale data is harmless and getting no answer is worse.
flashcards.more: In the same app, withdrawing a balance is CP (503 with Retry-After if unsure), and a like count is AP (a 30-second stale cache). The one question: "Which is more harmful, a wrong answer or no answer?"

flashcards.q: Why does a CP withdraw endpoint need an idempotency key?
flashcards.a: On a connection error you can't tell if the withdrawal happened. The client retries, and without a key the money could be paid out twice.
flashcards.more: The 503 with Retry-After tells the client to try again, which is exactly when a double payout can sneak in. The key lets the ledger recognize the repeat and return the first result instead of paying again.

flashcards.q: Why is "last write wins" (LWW) dangerous in AP?
flashcards.a: When both sides change something at once, one change is lost silently, and the side with the clock further ahead wins. Clocks aren't exact.
flashcards.more: The fix is a per-feature merge rule (for a cart, combine the items from both sides) or a data structure like a CRDT, where changes merge naturally. AP means "we'll reconcile later", so the rule has to be settled in advance.

flashcards.q: What is a tombstone in a merge rule, and why use one?
flashcards.a: A marker that an item was deleted. Without it, merging a side that still has the item brings the deleted item back.
flashcards.more: A merge that only takes the larger quantity per product can only add. The tombstone lets a delete survive the merge. The price: remove beats add, so a re-added product needs a new line id.
